oneLiner: Turn any long web address into a short link you can share anywhere, and count every click.

before: Long web addresses with tracking codes wrap across three lines in an email and look like spam.
Nobody can type a 90-character address off a flyer, a slide, or a podcast mention.
Long links eat into character limits in social posts and text messages.
You post the same page in five places and cannot tell which one actually sent people.
after: One short, tidy link that fits anywhere and looks trustworthy.
People who tap or type it land on the right page almost instantly.
Give each channel its own short link and compare the click counts side by side.
Counts show up a few seconds after each click, with no extra setup.

flowCaption: Paste a long link, share the short one, and watch the clicks add up while every visitor lands on the right page.

useCases.title: Find out which channel actually brings people in
useCases.situation: A product launch page is going out in the newsletter, on LinkedIn, on Instagram, and in a paid ad.
useCases.action: Make one short link per channel, all pointing to the same launch page.
useCases.result: A side-by-side click count for each channel, so next month's budget goes to what worked.
useCases.without: Everyone shares the same long link and the team argues about which channel drove the traffic.

useCases.title: Clean links in social posts
useCases.situation: A social media manager is writing a post where every character counts and an ugly link hurts clicks.
useCases.action: Shortens the campaign address before pasting it into the post.
useCases.result: A tidy link that leaves room for the message and still counts clicks.
useCases.without: A long address full of tracking codes that looks suspicious and crowds out the copy.

useCases.title: Know whether the prospect opened what you sent
useCases.situation: A rep emails a prospect a link to a case study after a discovery call.
useCases.action: Sends a fresh short link made just for that prospect's follow-up email.
useCases.result: If the click count moves from 0 to 1, the rep knows it is a good moment to follow up.
useCases.without: The rep guesses, and either chases too early or lets the deal go cold.

useCases.title: Links people can type from a flyer, slide, or booth banner
useCases.situation: A trade-show banner, a printed brochure, or the last slide of a webinar needs to send people to a sign-up page.
useCases.action: Prints the short link instead of the full address.
useCases.result: Visitors can actually type it, and the team sees how many people came from the printed piece.
useCases.without: Nobody types a long address, and print results are invisible.

useCases.title: Text message campaigns
useCases.situation: A promotion goes out by SMS, where long links break across lines and use up the character limit.
useCases.action: Uses a short link in the message.
useCases.result: A shorter, cleaner text and a count of how many recipients tapped through.
useCases.without: Messages split into two texts or the link gets cut off.

useCases.title: Compare which partners send real traffic
useCases.situation: Five resellers each promote the same offer to their own audiences.
useCases.action: Gives each partner their own short link to the offer page.
useCases.result: A click count per partner, useful in quarterly business reviews.
useCases.without: Every partner claims credit and there is nothing to compare.

useCases.title: A link you can say out loud
useCases.situation: A sponsor read on a podcast or a mention in a keynote needs to send listeners somewhere.
useCases.action: Reads out a short link instead of a long web address.
useCases.result: Listeners remember it, and the click count shows whether the spot worked.
useCases.without: Listeners give up halfway through hearing a long address.

useCases.title: Tidy links in chats and help replies
useCases.situation: A support agent shares a help article or onboarding guide in chat or email.
useCases.action: Shares a short link to the article.
useCases.result: A clean reply, and the team can see which help articles customers actually open.
useCases.without: Messy links in replies and no idea whether customers read the help content.

explanations.text: It is like a forwarding address for a web page. You hand out a short, easy address, and anyone who goes there is sent straight on to the real page. It also keeps a tally of how many people came through the door.

Every campaign link becomes measurable. Instead of guessing which email, post, partner, or flyer worked, you get a click count for each one and can move budget to what actually drives traffic, at no extra effort for the team.

Make one short link per channel for the same landing page. Share them, then check the counts: you will see in plain numbers whether the newsletter, LinkedIn, or the trade-show banner is pulling its weight.
Send each prospect their own short link to the material you promised. When the count ticks up, you know they opened it, and that is your cue to follow up while you are top of mind.
Short, trustworthy links for every campaign, with click counts that show which channels earn their budget.

script.hook: Quick question: which of our last campaign's channels sent the most people to the page? If the room hesitates, that is the problem this solves.
setup: Remember and say up front: this is a design, not a live product yet. You are showing the journey.
Have this page open on the sketch section, ready to share your screen.
Have a real long campaign link (with tracking codes) copied, and your phone's messaging app open.
Prepare one slide with three channels and illustrative click counts, for example Newsletter 412, LinkedIn 1,280, Banner 95, clearly labelled as example numbers.
Pick the framing from 'Ways to explain it' that fits your room.

steps.do: Ask the hook question, then say this is a planned product shown as a design.
steps.say: Today I'll show you what this will let you do. It's still at design stage, so we're walking the journey, not clicking through an app.

steps.do: Paste the long campaign link into a text to yourself and show how it wraps.
steps.say: This is what we send customers today. Would you tap on that? Would you type it off a banner?

steps.do: Share the sketch and trace it left to right with your cursor.
steps.say: You paste the long link, you get a short one back. Customers tap it and land on the right page almost instantly, and a few seconds later the click shows up in your count.

steps.do: Show the slide with three channels and their example click counts side by side.
steps.say: Same landing page, three short links. Now you can see in plain numbers that LinkedIn sent three times more people than the newsletter. That is a budget decision you can make with evidence.

steps.do: Scroll to the use cases and point to the card that matches someone in the room.
steps.say: For sales, it's knowing when a prospect opened your follow-up. For events, it's a link people can actually type off a banner.

steps.do: Scroll to 'What it is not for' and name the two biggest limits, then open the floor.
steps.say: To be clear about what it won't do: it counts clicks, it doesn't tell you who clicked. What would you use it for first?

questions.a: Not yet. It exists as a design that the engineering team has planned out. This demo shows how it is meant to work so you can tell us which uses matter most before it is built.

questions.q: Will the short link slow people down?
questions.a: No. The design target is under a twentieth of a second to send someone on to the real page, which is faster than people can notice. Recently used links are kept ready in fast memory so most clicks never wait.

questions.q: Why do the click counts show up a few seconds late?
questions.a: That is on purpose. Clicks are tallied in the background so that the person clicking is never kept waiting. The trade-off is that counts trail real clicks by a few seconds.

questions.q: Can I see who clicked, or where they were?
questions.a: Not in the current design. It counts clicks per link; it does not identify people, locations, or devices. If you need that, tell us, because it would be a separate decision with privacy implications.

questions.q: Can I choose the words in the link, like our-brand/spring-sale?
questions.a: The current design creates a short code for you. Custom names are not part of it yet, so do not promise them; capture the request instead.

questions.q: If I print a link and the page moves, can I change where it points?
questions.a: Editing a link's destination is not in the current design. For printed material, point the link at a page you expect to keep, and raise it as a request if this matters to you.

questions.q: What if it goes down? Will printed links break?
questions.a: Keeping links working is a top priority in the design. If the fast memory layer fails, links still work from the main records, and a backup copy of those records is planned.

questions.q: Could spammers use it to hide bad links?
questions.a: The design plans for that with limits on how many links one person can create quickly and a list of blocked destinations.

notFor: It is not live yet: this is a design, so there is nothing to sign up for or try today.
It counts clicks per link; it does not tell you who clicked, where they were, or what device they used.
Counts trail real clicks by a few seconds, so it is not a to-the-second live feed.
Custom words in the link, editing a link after sharing it, and QR codes are not in the current design.
It is not a full analytics or campaign-management tool; it tells you which links got clicks, not what people did afterwards.
Pricing, plans, and launch timing are not decided. Check with the product team before the demo and do not quote any.
It is designed for about 10,000 new links and a million clicks a day, with a plan to grow; check before promising it for a very large campaign.
